about: Histology in Cambridge Part IA (Medical and Veterinary Sciences Triposes) teaches the microscopic structure of cells, tissues and organs, with emphasis on how structure relates to function. It is taught through practical classes (2–4pm on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, according to the department's supervisor page), with images and computer modules on Moodle, and is a required part of 2nd MB. It is examined within the Homeostasis exam and its marks are combined with Homeostasis: in the 2023–24 format document (the latest found), the histology paper (HOM 2P) was a 1-hour paper of 30 multiple-choice questions worth 20% of the 2nd MB result and 10% of the Tripos result; check the current notice, as formats can change. The topics and their order follow the ten practical classes in the 2010–11 lecture list, the latest published list found.
topics: Introduction to microscopy and cell structure
Connective tissue, nerve and neuromuscular junction

notes.body:
Histology is the study of tissues at microscopic level, and at Cambridge it is learned in practical classes where you identify tissues on slides and electron micrographs and explain how structure serves function. Much of the exam is recognition, so you need a reliable method for looking at a slide.

Preparing tissue
- Fixation (commonly formaldehyde) cross-links proteins to preserve structure; tissue is then dehydrated, embedded in paraffin wax, cut into thin sections (a few micrometres) and stained.
- For electron microscopy, tissue is fixed (often with glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide), embedded in resin and cut into much thinner sections.
- Every step can introduce artefacts: shrinkage spaces, folds, knife marks and lost lipid (fat cells look empty in routine sections because the lipid dissolves during processing).

Stains
- Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) is the standard stain. Haematoxylin behaves as a basic dye and stains acidic structures (DNA in nuclei, RNA in ribosome-rich cytoplasm) blue-purple; these are called basophilic. Eosin is an acidic dye that stains basic structures (most cytoplasmic proteins, collagen) pink; these are eosinophilic.
- Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stains carbohydrate-rich material magenta: glycogen, mucins in goblet cells and basement membranes.
- Other stains highlight specific components: elastic stains (for example Verhoeff's) for elastic fibres, silver stains for reticular fibres, and immunohistochemistry for specific proteins.

Microscopes
- The light microscope can resolve about 0.2 µm, limited by the wavelength of light. The transmission electron microscope resolves far smaller detail (around a nanometre in biological specimens), showing organelles and membranes. The scanning electron microscope shows surfaces in three dimensions.
- A useful scale: a red blood cell is about 7–8 µm across, which helps you estimate the size of other cells.

Interpreting sections
- A section is a thin two-dimensional slice of a three-dimensional object. A tube can appear as a ring, an oval or a long strip depending on the angle of cut, and a nucleus may be missed if the cut misses it.
- Start at low power to identify the organ and its layers, then move to high power to identify cell types.

Cell structure seen in histology
- Nucleus: heterochromatin stains darkly, euchromatin pale. A large pale nucleus with a prominent nucleolus suggests an active cell (for example a neuron).
- Cytoplasm full of rough ER is basophilic (plasma cells, pancreatic acinar cells); cytoplasm full of mitochondria or smooth ER is eosinophilic (for example cells of the proximal tubule or the adrenal cortex).
- Golgi apparatus may show as a pale "negative image" next to the nucleus in plasma cells.
- Electron micrographs show mitochondria (cristae), rough ER, Golgi stacks, secretory granules, lysosomes, junctional complexes and microvilli, and you are expected to identify them.

Exam tips: in the practical exam, state what features you see before naming the tissue, and know which features distinguish look-alikes (for example, ureter versus vas deferens, or thyroid versus lactating breast).

notes.h: Connective tissue, nerve and the neuromuscular junction
notes.body:
Connective tissue supports and connects other tissues; nerve tissue carries signals; the neuromuscular junction transmits the signal from nerve to skeletal muscle.

Connective tissue components
- Cells: fibroblasts (make fibres and ground substance), adipocytes, macrophages, mast cells (granules with histamine and heparin), plasma cells and other immune cells.
- Fibres: collagen (pink on H&E, strong in tension), elastic fibres (need special stains, allow recoil) and reticular fibres (fine type III collagen, best seen with silver stains, forming the framework of lymphoid organs, liver and bone marrow).
- Ground substance: glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans and glycoproteins that bind water.
- Main collagen types: type I in skin, tendon, bone and ligaments; type II in hyaline and elastic cartilage; type III in reticular fibres and blood vessel walls; type IV in basement membranes (forms a network, not fibres).

Types of connective tissue
- Loose (areolar) connective tissue: plenty of cells and ground substance, under epithelia (for example the lamina propria).
- Dense irregular: collagen bundles in many directions, as in the dermis.
- Dense regular: parallel collagen bundles with flattened fibroblasts between them, as in tendons and ligaments.
- Specialised forms: adipose tissue, cartilage (hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage), bone and blood.

Cartilage and bone in brief
- Hyaline cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae, often in small groups (isogenous groups), in a glassy, basophilic matrix. It is avascular and surrounded by perichondrium (except at articular surfaces).
- Bone: compact bone is built of osteons, with concentric lamellae round a central (Haversian) canal; osteocytes lie in lacunae connected by canaliculi. Osteoblasts make bone; osteoclasts (large, multinucleated) resorb it.

Peripheral nerve
- In transverse section a nerve shows fascicles surrounded by perineurium, with epineurium around the whole nerve and endoneurium between axons.
- On H&E, myelin is partly dissolved, leaving a pale ring round each axon. Osmium preserves myelin and stains it black.
- Myelinated axons show nodes of Ranvier between internodes; each internode in the PNS is made by one Schwann cell. Unmyelinated axons sit in groups within the folds of a Schwann cell (Remak bundles).
- Ganglia contain large neuronal cell bodies, each surrounded by small satellite cells. Dorsal root ganglion neurons are pseudounipolar.

The neuromuscular junction
- A motor axon loses its myelin and ends in terminal boutons in a shallow depression on the muscle fibre (the motor end plate).
- Presynaptic terminals contain many synaptic vesicles (acetylcholine) and mitochondria.
- The postsynaptic membrane forms junctional folds. Acetylcholine receptors are concentrated at the crests of the folds, and voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated in the depths, helping to trigger an action potential.
- Acetylcholinesterase sits in the synaptic basal lamina and rapidly breaks down acetylcholine.
- Myasthenia gravis: antibodies (most commonly against acetylcholine receptors) reduce the number of functional receptors, causing fatigable weakness.

Exam tips: be able to identify tendon versus smooth muscle (both pink and elongated; tendon nuclei are flattened and squeezed between collagen bundles), and draw a labelled neuromuscular junction from an electron micrograph.

All three types of muscle convert chemical energy into force using actin and myosin, but their structure differs in ways that reflect how they are controlled.

Skeletal muscle
- Long, cylindrical, multinucleated fibres formed by fusion of myoblasts; nuclei lie at the periphery, just under the sarcolemma.
- Cross-striations reflect the regular arrangement of sarcomeres. The A band (dark, anisotropic) is the length of the thick myosin filaments; the I band (light) contains only thin actin filaments and is bisected by the Z line; the H zone is the central part of the A band with no overlap; the M line is in the middle of the H zone.
- During contraction the sarcomere shortens: the I band and H zone narrow, but the A band stays the same length (the sliding filament mechanism).
- T-tubules (invaginations of the sarcolemma) lie at the A–I junction in mammalian skeletal muscle and are flanked by two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum, forming triads.
- Connective tissue: endomysium around each fibre, perimysium around fascicles and epimysium around the muscle.
- Fibre types: slow oxidative fibres (many mitochondria and myoglobin; fatigue-resistant) and fast glycolytic fibres (fewer mitochondria; fatigue quickly).
- Satellite cells beneath the basal lamina are stem cells that allow repair.

Cardiac muscle
- Branching cells with one or two centrally placed nuclei, often with a pale perinuclear zone (sometimes containing lipofuscin in older people).
- Striated, with the same sarcomere structure as skeletal muscle.
- Cells are joined end to end by intercalated discs, which contain adherens junctions and desmosomes (mechanical coupling, in the transverse parts) and gap junctions (electrical coupling, mainly in the longitudinal parts). Gap junctions allow the heart to contract as a functional syncytium.
- T-tubules are wider and lie at the Z lines; the sarcoplasmic reticulum is less extensive and contacts tubules as dyads.
- Very many mitochondria reflect continuous aerobic work.
- Adult cardiac muscle cells have very limited capacity to regenerate, so infarcted muscle is replaced by scar. The extent to which new cardiomyocytes are made in adult life is an active research question.
- Purkinje fibres are specialised conducting cells: large, pale (glycogen-rich) and with few myofibrils.

Smooth muscle
- Spindle-shaped cells with a single central nucleus; no striations because actin and myosin are not arranged in sarcomeres. Thin filaments attach to dense bodies in the cytoplasm and dense plaques on the membrane.
- During contraction the cell shortens and the nucleus may look corkscrew-shaped.
- Cells are often coupled by gap junctions and contract slowly and economically, with calcium acting through calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase rather than troponin.
- Found in the walls of blood vessels, the gut, airways, bladder and uterus, usually under autonomic and hormonal control.
- In transverse section, smooth muscle shows profiles of different sizes, with nuclei visible only in the widest profiles (cut through the middle of the cell).

Exam tips: be ready to compare the three types in a table (shape, nuclei, striations, junctions, T-tubules, regeneration, control) and to identify the bands of a sarcomere on an electron micrograph.

Vessels change their wall structure along the circulation to match the pressures and functions at each level; blood cells are identified on smears by size, nucleus and granules.

General plan of vessel walls
- Tunica intima: endothelium on a basal lamina with a little subendothelial connective tissue; in arteries an internal elastic lamina marks its outer limit.
- Tunica media: smooth muscle and elastic tissue, arranged mostly circumferentially.
- Tunica adventitia: connective tissue, carrying vasa vasorum and nerves in larger vessels.

Arteries
- Elastic (conducting) arteries such as the aorta have many fenestrated elastic lamellae in the media. They stretch during systole and recoil in diastole, smoothing flow (the Windkessel effect).
- Muscular (distributing) arteries have a prominent internal elastic lamina and a thick media mainly of smooth muscle, controlling flow to organs.
- Arterioles have one to a few layers of smooth muscle and are the main site of peripheral resistance.

Capillaries
- Continuous capillaries (muscle, lung, CNS, where tight junctions form the blood–brain barrier) have an unbroken endothelium and basal lamina.
- Fenestrated capillaries (kidney glomerulus, endocrine glands, gut mucosa) have pores in the endothelium for rapid exchange.
- Sinusoids (discontinuous capillaries) in the liver, spleen and bone marrow are wide, with gaps between cells and an incomplete basal lamina, allowing cells and large molecules to pass.
- Pericytes wrap around capillaries and venules.

Veins
- Larger lumen and thinner, less organised wall than the accompanying artery; often collapsed or irregular in sections. The adventitia is usually the thickest layer.
- Valves, folds of intima, are present in medium-sized veins of the limbs.
- Post-capillary venules are where white cells leave the blood in inflammation; in lymph nodes, high endothelial venules allow lymphocytes to enter.

Lymphatic vessels have very thin walls, valves and no red cells in the lumen.

Blood
- Red blood cells: biconcave, anucleate discs about 7–8 µm across, living about 120 days.
- Neutrophils: the commonest white cell, with a multilobed nucleus (three to five lobes) and fine granules; first responders to bacterial infection.
- Lymphocytes: small cells with a round, dark nucleus and a thin rim of pale blue cytoplasm.
- Monocytes: the largest white cells, with a kidney-shaped or folded nucleus; they become macrophages in tissues.
- Eosinophils: bilobed nucleus and large orange-red granules; raised in parasitic infection and allergy.
- Basophils: the rarest, with large dark blue-purple granules that often obscure the nucleus; contain histamine.
- Platelets: small anucleate fragments of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.
- In adults, blood cells are made in red marrow (haematopoiesis), mainly in the axial skeleton and proximal ends of long bones.

Exam tips: be able to tell an artery from its companion vein in one section (thick muscular wall with a wavy internal elastic lamina versus thin wall and wide lumen), and rank the white cells by abundance.

Epithelia cover surfaces and line cavities and ducts. Their shape and layering tell you what job they do, and skin is the best example of an epithelium specialised for protection.

General features of epithelia
- Cells sit on a basement membrane, are closely packed with little extracellular matrix, are avascular (fed by diffusion from underlying connective tissue) and are polarised, with apical and basolateral surfaces.
- Junctions: tight junctions (seal the gap between cells), adherens junctions and desmosomes (mechanical attachment), gap junctions (communication) and hemidesmosomes (anchor cells to the basement membrane).
- Apical specialisations: microvilli (absorption, the brush border), cilia (motile, with a 9+2 microtubule pattern, moving mucus or eggs) and stereocilia (long microvilli, not true cilia, in the epididymis).

Classification
- By number of layers: simple (one) or stratified (more than one). Pseudostratified epithelium is one layer whose nuclei lie at different heights, so it looks stratified; all cells touch the basement membrane.
- By the shape of the surface cells: squamous, cuboidal or columnar.
- Examples: simple squamous (endothelium, alveoli, mesothelium); simple cuboidal (kidney tubules, thyroid follicles); simple columnar (stomach, intestine); pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells (trachea and bronchi); stratified squamous non-keratinised (oesophagus, vagina); stratified squamous keratinised (epidermis); urothelium (transitional epithelium), which lines the urinary tract and has large dome-shaped surface cells that flatten when the bladder stretches.

Glands
- Exocrine glands secrete via ducts; endocrine glands secrete into the blood.
- Modes of secretion: merocrine (exocytosis, most glands), apocrine (part of the apical cytoplasm is lost, for example lipid in the mammary gland) and holocrine (the whole cell disintegrates, as in sebaceous glands).

Skin
- Epidermis (keratinised stratified squamous epithelium) from deep to superficial: stratum basale (dividing cells), stratum spinosum (cells joined by many desmosomes, looking "prickly" after shrinkage), stratum granulosum (keratohyalin granules), stratum lucidum (only in thick skin of palms and soles) and stratum corneum (dead, flattened, keratin-filled cells).
- Other epidermal cells: melanocytes in the basal layer transfer melanin to keratinocytes; Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting cells; Merkel cells are associated with touch.
- Dermis: a papillary layer of loose connective tissue interdigitating with the epidermis, and a deeper reticular layer of dense irregular connective tissue.
- Appendages: hair follicles with sebaceous glands and arrector pili muscle; eccrine sweat glands (coiled secretory portion with a duct lined by two layers of cuboidal cells); apocrine sweat glands in the axilla and groin.
- Thick skin (palms and soles) has a very thick stratum corneum and no hair follicles; thin skin has hair follicles.

Clinical links
- Blistering diseases target junctions: pemphigus vulgaris involves antibodies against desmosomal proteins (splitting within the epidermis), and bullous pemphigoid antibodies target hemidesmosome proteins (splitting beneath the epidermis).
- Squamous metaplasia, as in the airways of smokers, is a change from one adult epithelium to another, more resilient type.

Exam tips: name an epithelium with three terms (layers, shape, specialisation) and give a site and a function for each.

The airway changes progressively from the trachea to the alveoli: cartilage, glands and goblet cells disappear, smooth muscle becomes relatively more prominent and then disappears, and the epithelium thins until it is barely thick enough to see.

Conducting portion
- Nasal cavity: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with a rich venous plexus that warms and humidifies air; olfactory epithelium in the roof.
- Trachea: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells on a thick basement membrane; submucosal seromucous glands; C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage open posteriorly, where the trachealis smooth muscle bridges the gap.
- Bronchi: similar epithelium, with plates of cartilage rather than rings and a layer of smooth muscle between the mucosa and the cartilage.
- Bronchioles (roughly 1 mm diameter and below): no cartilage and no glands; the epithelium becomes simple columnar then cuboidal; goblet cells are lost and club cells (formerly Clara cells) appear. Club cells secrete protective proteins (including some surfactant proteins) and act as progenitor cells. The smooth muscle layer is relatively thick, which is why bronchoconstriction in asthma narrows these small airways so much.
- Terminal bronchioles are the last purely conducting airways.

Respiratory portion
- Respiratory bronchioles have alveoli opening from their walls; they lead into alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli.
- Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin squamous cells covering most (around 95%) of the alveolar surface and forming part of the gas exchange barrier.
- Type II pneumocytes are rounded cells with lamellar bodies that secrete surfactant. They also divide to replace type I cells after injury. Although they cover only a small fraction of the surface area, they actually outnumber type I cells.
- Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) clear particles from alveoli.
- The blood–air barrier, where thinnest, consists of type I cell, fused basal laminae and capillary endothelium, only a fraction of a micrometre thick.
- Interalveolar septa contain capillaries, elastic fibres (for recoil) and occasional pores (of Kohn) connecting alveoli.

Mucociliary clearance
- Goblet cells and glands produce mucus; cilia beat in a coordinated way to move it upward at a steady rate towards the pharynx, where it is swallowed.
- Impairment occurs in smoking (ciliary loss and squamous metaplasia), primary ciliary dyskinesia (abnormal ciliary structure) and cystic fibrosis (thick, dehydrated mucus because of defective CFTR chloride channels).

Clinical links
- Surfactant deficiency in premature babies causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
- Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, reducing surface area and elastic recoil.
- Chronic bronchitis features enlarged submucosal glands and goblet cell hyperplasia.

Exam tips: build a table down the airway listing epithelium, goblet cells, glands, cartilage and smooth muscle at each level; this is a favourite way of testing identification.

notes.h: The urinary system and the adrenal gland
notes.body:
The kidney is easy to recognise at low power by its glomeruli, and each part of the nephron has an appearance that fits its job. The adrenal gland sits on top of the kidney and is usually taught alongside it.

Kidney organisation
- Cortex contains the renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules; medulla contains the loops of Henle and collecting ducts arranged in medullary pyramids.
- Renal corpuscle: a capillary tuft (glomerulus) inside Bowman's capsule. The visceral layer of the capsule consists of podocytes, whose interdigitating foot processes are separated by filtration slits bridged by slit diaphragms. The parietal layer is simple squamous epithelium. Mesangial cells support the capillaries and can phagocytose.
- Glomerular filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, a thick glomerular basement membrane and the podocyte slit diaphragms; it restricts passage by size and charge.

Tubules
- Proximal convoluted tubule: cuboidal cells with a tall brush border (microvilli), eosinophilic cytoplasm packed with mitochondria and basal infoldings; the lumen often looks fuzzy and indistinct. It reabsorbs most of the filtered sodium, water, glucose and amino acids.
- Loop of Henle: thin limbs lined by simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb with cuboidal cells.
- Distal convoluted tubule: smaller, paler cuboidal cells, no brush border and a clearer lumen; more nuclei visible per cross-section than in the proximal tubule.
- Macula densa: a patch of closely packed, tall cells in the tubule wall at the end of the thick ascending limb, where it returns to touch its own glomerulus (classically described as part of the distal tubule); it senses tubular sodium chloride.
- Juxtaglomerular cells: modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole that secrete renin. With the macula densa and extraglomerular mesangial cells they form the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
- Collecting ducts: cuboidal to columnar cells with clear cell boundaries; principal cells respond to antidiuretic hormone (inserting aquaporin-2) and aldosterone; intercalated cells regulate acid–base balance.

The urinary tract
- Ureter, bladder and proximal urethra are lined by urothelium. The ureter has a star-shaped lumen and smooth muscle layers; the bladder wall has thick interwoven bundles of smooth muscle (detrusor).

The adrenal gland
- Capsule, then cortex, then medulla.
- Zona glomerulosa: small cells in rounded clusters just under the capsule; secrete mineralocorticoids (aldosterone).
- Zona fasciculata: the thickest zone; columns of large pale cells full of lipid droplets (they look foamy or vacuolated); secrete glucocorticoids (cortisol).
- Zona reticularis: a network of cords of smaller, more eosinophilic cells, often with lipofuscin; secrete adrenal androgens (and some cortisol).
- Medulla: chromaffin cells, modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons, secreting adrenaline and noradrenaline; they receive preganglionic sympathetic fibres directly.
- The cortex is derived from mesoderm, while the medulla is derived from neural crest.
- Blood flows from the capsule through the cortex to the medulla, so medullary cells are exposed to high cortisol levels, which promotes the conversion of noradrenaline to adrenaline.

Clinical links
- Damage to podocytes or the basement membrane causes protein leak (nephrotic syndrome).
- Hypersecretion of cortisol (Cushing's syndrome) or aldosterone (Conn's syndrome) can arise from tumours of the relevant zone; phaeochromocytoma is a tumour of chromaffin cells.

Exam tips: the proximal versus distal tubule distinction is a classic identification question; learn the features as a list (cell height, brush border, lumen, staining, number of nuclei).

The gut tube from oesophagus to anal canal has the same four-layer plan throughout, and the differences between regions reflect what each part does.

The general plan
- Mucosa: epithelium, lamina propria (loose connective tissue with lymphoid cells and capillaries) and muscularis mucosae (thin smooth muscle).
- Submucosa: dense connective tissue with larger vessels, the submucosal (Meissner's) plexus and, in places, glands.
- Muscularis externa: usually inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle, with the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus between them.
- Serosa (mesothelium on connective tissue) where the gut is intraperitoneal, or adventitia where it is attached to surrounding structures.

Oesophagus
- Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium; oesophageal glands in the submucosa.
- The muscularis externa changes from skeletal muscle in the upper third to smooth muscle in the lower third, with a mixture in between.
- Barrett's oesophagus is metaplasia of the lower oesophageal lining to columnar epithelium with goblet cells after chronic acid reflux.

Stomach
- Simple columnar surface mucous cells line the surface and gastric pits.
- Gastric glands in the body and fundus contain parietal (oxyntic) cells, which are large, eosinophilic and pyramidal, secreting hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor; chief (zymogenic) cells, which are basophilic and basal in the glands, secreting pepsinogen; mucous neck cells; and enteroendocrine cells. G cells, secreting gastrin, are concentrated in the antrum.
- The muscularis externa has an extra inner oblique layer.
- Loss of parietal cells in autoimmune gastritis reduces intrinsic factor, leading to vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia).

Small intestine
- Surface area is enlarged by circular folds (plicae circulares), villi and microvilli.
- Enterocytes (absorptive columnar cells with a brush border), goblet cells, enteroendocrine cells and, at the base of the crypts of Lieberkühn, stem cells and Paneth cells (with eosinophilic granules containing antimicrobial proteins such as lysozyme and defensins).
- Duodenum: Brunner's glands in the submucosa secrete alkaline mucus to neutralise acid.
- Jejunum: tall, finger-like villi and prominent plicae.
- Ileum: shorter villi, more goblet cells and Peyer's patches (aggregated lymphoid follicles in the mucosa and submucosa). M cells over the patches sample antigens.
- Coeliac disease flattens the villi (villous atrophy) with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

Large intestine
- No villi; straight tubular crypts with many goblet cells; the absorptive cells absorb water and electrolytes.
- The outer longitudinal muscle is gathered into three bands, the taeniae coli.
- The appendix has a ring of lymphoid follicles in its mucosa and submucosa.

Anal canal
- The epithelium changes from colorectal columnar epithelium to stratified squamous (non-keratinised, then keratinised at the anal verge). The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of circular smooth muscle.

Exam tips: identify the region from the epithelium and any distinctive feature (Brunner's glands, Peyer's patches, taeniae coli, skeletal muscle in the oesophagus).

These are the main glands associated with the gut. Each is built from secretory units, ducts and connective tissue, and the arrangement reflects whether the gland is exocrine, endocrine or both.

Liver
- Hepatocytes are large polygonal cells with central round nuclei (sometimes two) and eosinophilic cytoplasm rich in mitochondria, smooth and rough ER and glycogen. They are arranged in plates, one to two cells thick, separated by sinusoids.
- Sinusoids carry mixed blood from the hepatic portal vein and hepatic artery towards the central vein. Their endothelium is fenestrated and discontinuous, with no proper basement membrane. Kupffer cells (macrophages) line the sinusoids.
- The space of Disse lies between endothelium and hepatocytes. It contains hepatic stellate cells, which store vitamin A and, when activated by chronic injury, produce collagen and cause fibrosis and cirrhosis.
- Bile canaliculi are tiny channels between adjacent hepatocytes, sealed by tight junctions. Bile flows in the opposite direction to blood, towards the portal tracts.
- Portal tracts (portal triads) contain a branch of the portal vein, a branch of the hepatic artery and a bile duct (lined by cuboidal epithelium), with lymphatics.

Ways of describing liver units
- Classic lobule: a hexagon centred on a central vein with portal tracts at its corners (emphasises blood drainage).
- Portal lobule: triangular, centred on a portal tract (emphasises bile drainage).
- Liver acinus: a diamond-shaped unit based on blood supply from the portal tract. Zone 1 (periportal) receives the most oxygenated blood; zone 3 (centrilobular, near the central vein) receives the least oxygen and contains most drug-metabolising enzymes, so it is most vulnerable to ischaemia and to some toxins, such as paracetamol overdose.

Pancreas
- Exocrine part: serous acini of pyramidal cells with basophilic basal cytoplasm (rough ER) and apical eosinophilic zymogen granules containing digestive enzymes or their inactive precursors.
- Centroacinar cells, the start of the duct system, sit within the acini; they and the duct cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid in response to secretin.
- The pancreas has no striated ducts, which helps distinguish it from the parotid gland.
- Endocrine part: islets of Langerhans, pale-staining clusters of cells scattered among the acini. Beta cells (insulin) are the most numerous; alpha cells secrete glucagon, delta cells somatostatin and PP cells pancreatic polypeptide. In human islets, the cell types are more intermingled than in the classic rodent pattern of a beta-cell core with a mantle of other cells.

Salivary glands
- Secretory units are serous (protein-rich watery secretion; round nuclei in the basal part of the cell and granular cytoplasm, basophilic basally) or mucous (pale, foamy cytoplasm with nuclei flattened at the base).
- Myoepithelial cells around acini contract to expel secretion.
- Ducts: intercalated ducts (small, low cuboidal), then striated ducts (columnar cells with basal striations from infoldings packed with mitochondria; they modify saliva by reabsorbing sodium chloride), then excretory ducts.
- Parotid gland: almost purely serous.
- Submandibular gland: mixed, mostly serous, with some mucous acini.
- Sublingual gland: mixed, mostly mucous.
- In mixed glands, serous "demilunes" capping mucous tubules are classically described. Studies using rapid-freezing fixation suggest that demilunes may be partly an artefact of conventional fixation, with serous cells normally lying in line with mucous cells, so treat the textbook picture with some caution.

Exam tips: be able to tell pancreas from parotid (islets and centroacinar cells but no striated ducts in pancreas) and to explain why zone 3 of the liver acinus is most vulnerable.

Endocrine glands have no ducts and secrete into a rich capillary network, usually fenestrated. Their histology reflects whether hormone is stored outside cells (thyroid), in granules (pituitary) or made on demand (steroid-secreting cells).

Thyroid gland
- Built of follicles: spheres of simple cuboidal epithelium (follicular cells) enclosing colloid, which is mainly thyroglobulin and stains pink.
- The height of the follicular cells reflects activity: flattened cells with abundant colloid suggest an inactive gland; tall cells with scanty, scalloped colloid suggest active hormone release, as under high TSH stimulation.
- Hormone synthesis: follicular cells take up iodide, which is oxidised and attached to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin in the colloid. Thyroglobulin is then taken back into the cell by endocytosis and broken down in lysosomes to release T4 (thyroxine) and T3.
- Parafollicular (C) cells lie between follicles or at their edges and are paler, larger cells that secrete calcitonin. They reach the thyroid via the ultimobranchial body. They were long taught to come from the neural crest, but lineage-tracing studies in mice suggest an endodermal origin, so their origin is now disputed.
- Clinical links: Graves' disease (stimulating antibodies to the TSH receptor; tall cells, reduced colloid), Hashimoto's thyroiditis (lymphocytic infiltration and follicle destruction) and medullary carcinoma (from C cells).

Parathyroid glands
- Usually four small glands behind the thyroid.
- Chief (principal) cells: small cells in cords or sheets that secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), raising blood calcium.
- Oxyphil cells: larger cells with intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm packed with mitochondria; their function is uncertain; they increase with age.
- Adipocytes increase in the gland with age.

Pituitary gland (hypophysis)
- Two parts with different origins: the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) develops from Rathke's pouch, an upgrowth of oral ectoderm; the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is a downgrowth of the diencephalon (neuroectoderm).
- Anterior pituitary: cords of cells among sinusoidal capillaries. On H&E, cells are classed as acidophils (somatotrophs making growth hormone and lactotrophs making prolactin), basophils (thyrotrophs making TSH, gonadotrophs making FSH and LH, and corticotrophs making ACTH, which are glycoproteins or derived from a glycoprotein precursor and PAS-positive) and chromophobes (cells with few granules). Immunohistochemistry is used to identify cell types precisely.
- The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary through releasing and inhibiting hormones carried in the hypophyseal portal system from capillaries in the median eminence to the sinusoids of the anterior lobe.
- Posterior pituitary: pale-staining, made of unmyelinated axons from the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, with pituicytes (glial cells). Hormones (antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin) are stored in axonal swellings called Herring bodies and released into fenestrated capillaries.
- Clinical links: pituitary adenomas may secrete excess hormone (for example prolactin or growth hormone) or compress the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia.

Exam tips: be able to explain follicle appearance in hypo- and hyperactive thyroid, and the different origins and control of the anterior and posterior pituitary.

cards.b: Staining with basic dyes such as haematoxylin (blue-purple): acidic structures such as nuclei (DNA) and rough ER/ribosomes (RNA).
Staining with the acidic dye eosin (pink): basic structures such as most cytoplasmic proteins, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm and collagen.
Carbohydrate-rich material, magenta: glycogen, mucins (goblet cells) and basement membranes.
About 0.2 µm, limited by the wavelength of visible light.

cards.f: Why do fat cells look empty on H&E?
cards.b: The lipid dissolves in solvents used during paraffin processing, leaving a clear space with a thin rim of cytoplasm.
A red blood cell, roughly 7–8 µm in diameter.

cards.f: Why is a plasma cell's cytoplasm basophilic?
cards.b: It is packed with rough ER whose ribosomal RNA binds haematoxylin; the Golgi shows as a pale area next to the nucleus.
Skin dermis, tendon, ligament and bone; the commonest collagen.
Hyaline and elastic cartilage.
Network-forming collagen of basement membranes (basal lamina); does not form fibres.
Fine type III collagen fibres, shown by silver stains; form the scaffold of lymph nodes, spleen, liver and bone marrow.
Parallel collagen bundles with rows of flattened fibroblasts between them; tendons and ligaments.
Small glial cells surrounding each neuronal cell body in a peripheral ganglion.

cards.f: Junctional folds of the motor end plate
cards.b: Postsynaptic folds: ACh receptors concentrated at the crests, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in the depths.

cards.f: Where is acetylcholinesterase at the NMJ?
cards.b: Anchored in the basal lamina of the synaptic cleft.

cards.f: Which sarcomere band stays constant during contraction?
cards.b: The A band (length of the thick filaments); the I band and H zone narrow.

cards.f: Position of nuclei in skeletal vs cardiac muscle
cards.b: Skeletal: many, peripheral. Cardiac: one or two, central.
Adherens junctions and desmosomes (mechanical) and gap junctions (electrical coupling).
A T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum, at the A–I junction in mammals.

cards.f: Location of T-tubules in cardiac muscle
cards.b: At the Z lines; wider than in skeletal muscle, forming dyads with the SR.
Cytoplasmic attachment points for thin filaments in smooth muscle, functionally similar to Z lines.
Stem cells between the sarcolemma and basal lamina that proliferate and fuse to repair fibres.
Large, pale, glycogen-rich conducting cardiac muscle cells with few myofibrils, in the subendocardium.

cards.f: Three tunics of a vessel wall
cards.b: Intima (endothelium and subendothelium), media (smooth muscle and elastic tissue) and adventitia (connective tissue).
Elastic: many elastic lamellae in media (aorta), recoil smooths flow. Muscular: thick smooth muscle media with prominent internal elastic lamina, distributes flow.
Arterioles, via contraction of their smooth muscle.
Continuous (muscle, lung, CNS), fenestrated (glomerulus, endocrine glands, gut) and sinusoidal/discontinuous (liver, spleen, marrow).
Nucleus with three to five lobes, pale cytoplasm with fine granules; the most abundant white cell in adults.
Bilobed nucleus, large orange-red granules; raised in parasitic infection and allergy.
About 120 days; old cells removed mainly by macrophages in the spleen.

cards.f: Where do leucocytes leave the blood in inflammation?
cards.b: Mainly through post-capillary venules.
A single layer in which every cell touches the basement membrane but nuclei lie at different heights, so it looks stratified (e.g. trachea).
Transitional epithelium of the urinary tract; large dome-shaped surface cells flatten as the bladder stretches and resist toxic urine.

cards.f: Layers of the epidermis (deep to superficial)
cards.b: Stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only), corneum.
The whole cell disintegrates to form the secretion; e.g. sebaceous glands.
Very long microvilli (not true cilia, no 9+2 axoneme); e.g. in the epididymis and inner-ear hair cells.
Antigen-presenting dendritic cells within the epidermis.
Junctions anchoring basal epithelial cells to the basement membrane; target in bullous pemphigoid.
Thick (palms, soles): thick stratum corneum, stratum lucidum, no hair. Thin: hair follicles and sebaceous glands, thinner keratin layer.
C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, open posteriorly where trachealis smooth muscle bridges the gap.

cards.f: How do bronchioles differ from bronchi?
cards.b: No cartilage and no submucosal glands; goblet cells lost and club cells appear; relatively prominent smooth muscle.
Non-ciliated dome-shaped cells in bronchioles; secrete protective proteins (including some surfactant proteins) and act as progenitors. Formerly called Clara cells.
Very thin squamous cells covering about 95% of the alveolar surface; part of the gas-exchange barrier.
Cuboidal cells with lamellar bodies; secrete surfactant and act as progenitors for type I cells.

cards.f: Layers of the thinnest blood–air barrier
cards.b: Type I pneumocyte, fused basal laminae, capillary endothelium.
The first part of the airway with alveoli opening from its wall, marking the start of the respiratory portion.
PCT: tall eosinophilic cells, brush border, fuzzy lumen, few nuclei per section. DCT: smaller paler cells, no brush border, clear lumen, more nuclei.
Fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms.
Macula densa (end of the thick ascending limb, classically called distal tubule), renin-secreting juxtaglomerular cells (afferent arteriole) and extraglomerular mesangial cells.
Senses NaCl delivery at the end of the thick ascending limb and signals to adjust afferent arteriolar tone and renin release.
Glomerulosa: aldosterone. Fasciculata: cortisol. Reticularis: adrenal androgens (and some cortisol).

cards.f: Why do zona fasciculata cells look foamy?
cards.b: They are packed with lipid droplets (cholesterol esters for steroid synthesis) that dissolve during processing.

cards.f: Embryological origin of the adrenal medulla
cards.b: Neural crest; chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons.
Respond to ADH (aquaporin-2 insertion) and aldosterone (sodium reabsorption).

cards.f: Four layers of the gut wall
cards.b: Mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa or adventitia.
Hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor (needed for vitamin B12 absorption).
Pepsinogen; chief cells are basophilic and lie at the base of gastric glands.
Submucosal glands of the duodenum secreting alkaline mucus to neutralise gastric acid.
Cells at the base of small intestinal crypts with eosinophilic granules containing antimicrobial proteins (e.g. lysozyme, defensins).
Aggregated lymphoid follicles in the ileal mucosa and submucosa, covered by M cells that sample antigens.
Skeletal in the upper third, mixed in the middle, smooth in the lower third.
Three longitudinal bands formed by the outer longitudinal muscle of the colon.
Branch of the portal vein, branch of the hepatic artery and bile duct (with lymphatics).
Resident macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids.
Cells in the space of Disse that store vitamin A; when activated by chronic injury they produce collagen, causing fibrosis.
Centrilobular zone near the central vein: least oxygenated and rich in drug-metabolising enzymes, so most vulnerable to ischaemia and some toxins.
Pale duct-origin cells inside pancreatic acini; with duct cells they secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid in response to secretin.
Beta cell, secreting insulin.
Salivary ducts lined by columnar cells with basal infoldings and mitochondria; reabsorb NaCl, making saliva hypotonic. Absent from pancreas.

cards.f: Which salivary gland is almost purely serous?
cards.b: The parotid gland.
Stored thyroglobulin in the follicle lumen; iodinated tyrosine residues on it are the precursors of T4 and T3.

cards.f: Signs of an active thyroid follicle
cards.b: Tall cuboidal to columnar cells, reduced colloid with scalloped edges (endocytosis).
Pale cells between thyroid follicles secreting calcitonin; origin of medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Small cells secreting parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium.

cards.f: Origin of anterior and posterior pituitary
cards.b: Anterior: Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm). Posterior: downgrowth of the diencephalon (neuroectoderm).
Somatotrophs (growth hormone) and lactotrophs (prolactin).
Thyrotrophs (TSH), gonadotrophs (FSH, LH) and corticotrophs (ACTH); PAS-positive.
Axonal swellings in the posterior pituitary storing ADH or oxytocin.

questions.q: In an H&E-stained section, which structure would appear most strongly basophilic?
options: The cytoplasm of a pancreatic acinar cell near its base
The cytoplasm of a skeletal muscle fibre
questions.why: The basal cytoplasm of pancreatic acinar cells is crowded with rough ER, and its RNA binds haematoxylin strongly. Collagen, muscle cytoplasm and red cells (full of haemoglobin) are eosinophilic.

questions.q: A tubular structure appears in one section as a circle and in another as a long strip. What is the best explanation?
options: The tube changes epithelium along its length
The two sections cut the same tube in transverse and longitudinal planes
One section is stained with PAS
questions.why: Sections are two-dimensional slices, and the appearance of a tube depends on the plane of section. Different tissues or stains do not explain a change from circle to strip, and nothing suggests a change in epithelium.

questions.q: Explain how haematoxylin and eosin produce the typical appearance of a routine histological section, giving examples of structures stained by each.
markScheme: Haematoxylin acts as a basic dye binding acidic (negatively charged) components: basophilic, blue-purple
Examples: nuclei (DNA), rough ER and ribosomes (RNA), cartilage matrix
Eosin is an acidic dye binding basic components: eosinophilic, pink
Examples: cytoplasmic proteins, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm, collagen, red blood cells
questions.modelAnswer: Haematoxylin, used with a mordant, behaves as a basic dye and binds negatively charged, acidic components, staining them blue-purple; these are described as basophilic. Nuclei stain because of their DNA, and cells rich in rough ER or free ribosomes, such as plasma cells and the basal parts of pancreatic acinar cells, stain because of their RNA; the sulphated matrix of hyaline cartilage is also basophilic. Eosin is an acidic dye that binds positively charged components, staining them pink; these are eosinophilic. Examples are most cytoplasmic proteins, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm such as that of proximal tubule cells, collagen fibres and red blood cells.

questions.q: Which collagen type forms the main structural network of basement membranes?
questions.why: Type IV collagen assembles into a sheet-like network in the basal lamina. Type I forms thick fibres in skin, tendon and bone, type II is in cartilage and type III forms reticular fibres.

questions.q: On an electron micrograph of a neuromuscular junction, where would acetylcholine receptors be most concentrated?
options: In the depths of the junctional folds
At the crests of the postsynaptic junctional folds
questions.why: Acetylcholine receptors cluster at the crests, directly opposite the release sites. The depths contain voltage-gated sodium channels, the presynaptic membrane carries calcium channels and release machinery, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium.

questions.q: Describe the histological features that allow you to distinguish a peripheral nerve from dense regular connective tissue (tendon) in an H&E section.
markScheme: Nerve: fascicles enclosed by perineurium; epineurium around nerve
Nerve fibres wavy; pale halo of dissolved myelin around central axon in transverse section
Schwann cell nuclei elongated but plumper, scattered within fascicles
Tendon: densely packed parallel collagen bundles, very eosinophilic, few rows of flattened fibroblast nuclei; no perineurium or myelin
questions.modelAnswer: A peripheral nerve is organised into fascicles, each bounded by a perineurium of flattened cells, with the epineurium wrapping the whole nerve. In longitudinal section the nerve fibres look wavy, and in transverse section each myelinated axon appears as a central dot within a pale ring where myelin was dissolved during processing; Schwann cell nuclei are scattered among the fibres. Tendon, by contrast, consists of tightly packed parallel bundles of collagen that stain intensely pink, with rows of flattened, dark fibroblast nuclei squeezed between the bundles, and has no fascicular perineurium or myelin halos.

questions.q: During shortening of a skeletal muscle sarcomere, which of the following stays the same length?
questions.why: The A band corresponds to the thick filaments, which do not change length as filaments slide. The I band and H zone narrow as overlap increases, and the Z lines move closer together.

questions.q: Which feature is characteristic of cardiac but not skeletal muscle?
questions.why: Intercalated discs join cardiac muscle cells end to end. Striations, T-tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum are found in both cardiac and skeletal muscle.

questions.q: Compare the structure of skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle as seen in the light microscope, and explain one functional consequence of each difference you describe.
markScheme: Skeletal: long multinucleate fibres, peripheral nuclei, striated: fast, voluntary, neural control of each motor unit
Cardiac: branched cells, central nuclei, striated, intercalated discs: gap junctions make a functional syncytium
Smooth: spindle cells, single central nucleus, no striations: slow, economical, sustained contraction
Regeneration: skeletal via satellite cells; cardiac very limited; smooth can divide
Correct link of structure to control (somatic vs autonomic/hormonal)
questions.modelAnswer: Skeletal muscle fibres are long, cylindrical and multinucleate with nuclei at the periphery and clear cross-striations. Each fibre is innervated individually as part of a motor unit, allowing fast, finely graded voluntary contraction, and satellite cells allow repair. Cardiac muscle cells are shorter and branched, with one or two central nuclei, striations and intercalated discs. Gap junctions in the discs couple cells electrically so the heart contracts as a functional syncytium, while desmosomes hold cells together under constant load; adult cardiomyocytes regenerate very poorly, so infarcts heal by scarring. Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus and no striations, because actin and myosin are not organised in sarcomeres. This allows slow, sustained and economical contraction over a wide range of lengths, controlled by autonomic nerves, hormones and local factors, and smooth muscle cells retain the ability to divide.

questions.q: Which type of capillary would you expect in the liver?
options: Fenestrated with a continuous basal lamina only
questions.why: Hepatic sinusoids have gaps between endothelial cells and little or no basal lamina, letting plasma reach hepatocytes freely. Continuous capillaries are found in muscle and brain, fenestrated ones in glomeruli and endocrine glands, and lymphatic capillaries are not part of the blood circulation.

questions.q: On a blood smear, a cell about twice the diameter of a red cell has a bilobed nucleus and large orange-red cytoplasmic granules. What is it?
questions.why: Bilobed nucleus with large eosinophilic granules defines the eosinophil. Neutrophils have three to five lobes and fine granules, basophils have dark blue-purple granules, and monocytes are larger with a folded nucleus and no prominent granules.

questions.q: Describe how you would distinguish a muscular artery from its accompanying vein in a transverse section.
markScheme: Artery: thick wall relative to lumen; round, regular profile
Artery: prominent wavy internal elastic lamina; media thickest layer of smooth muscle
Vein: thinner wall, wider and often collapsed/irregular lumen
Vein: adventitia usually thickest layer; little elastic tissue; may show valves
questions.modelAnswer: A muscular artery has a thick wall in relation to its lumen and usually keeps a round, regular profile. Its intima is marked by a prominent, wavy internal elastic lamina, and the media is the thickest layer, made of many layers of circular smooth muscle. The accompanying vein has a much thinner wall and a wider lumen, often collapsed or irregular in shape, with a poorly defined media and an adventitia that is usually the thickest layer. Veins lack a clear internal elastic lamina and may show valves as folds of the intima.

questions.q: Which epithelium lines the oesophagus?
questions.why: The oesophagus is lined by moist, non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium that resists abrasion by swallowed food. Simple columnar epithelium lines the stomach and intestines, pseudostratified ciliated epithelium lines the airways and keratinised epithelium is found in the epidermis.

questions.q: In which layer of the epidermis are cells joined by numerous desmosomes, giving them a 'prickly' appearance in routine sections?
questions.why: Shrinkage during processing pulls cells apart except at desmosomes, producing the spiny appearance of the stratum spinosum. The basal layer contains dividing cells on the basement membrane, the granular layer shows keratohyalin granules and the stratum corneum consists of dead, flattened cells.

questions.q: Name four types of epithelium, giving one site and one function linked to the structure of each.
markScheme: Simple squamous, e.g. alveoli/endothelium: thin for diffusion
Simple columnar with microvilli, e.g. small intestine: absorption/secretion
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells, e.g. trachea: mucociliary clearance
Stratified squamous (keratinised skin / non-keratinised oesophagus): protection against abrasion; urothelium: stretch and impermeability
questions.modelAnswer: Simple squamous epithelium, such as that lining the alveoli and blood vessels, is extremely thin, allowing rapid diffusion of gases and solutes. Simple columnar epithelium with a microvillous brush border lines the small intestine, where the tall cells and large surface area suit absorption and secretion. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines the trachea and bronchi; goblet cells secrete mucus that traps particles and cilia sweep it towards the pharynx. Stratified squamous epithelium protects against abrasion: keratinised in the epidermis to resist drying and mechanical damage, non-keratinised in the oesophagus where the surface is kept moist.

questions.q: Which feature would identify a bronchiole rather than a small bronchus?
options: Absence of cartilage and submucosal glands
questions.why: Bronchioles lack cartilage and glands. Smooth muscle occurs in both, and pseudostratified ciliated epithelium and goblet cells are features of bronchi, being lost along the bronchioles.

questions.q: Which cell produces pulmonary surfactant?
questions.why: Type II pneumocytes store and secrete surfactant from lamellar bodies. Type I cells form the thin gas-exchange surface, macrophages clear particles and goblet cells secrete mucus in larger airways.

questions.q: Describe the changes in airway wall structure from the trachea to the alveoli.
markScheme: Trachea: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, goblet cells, seromucous glands, C-shaped hyaline cartilage, trachealis
Bronchi: same epithelium, cartilage plates, smooth muscle layer, glands
Bronchioles: no cartilage/glands, simple columnar→cuboidal epithelium, club cells replace goblet cells, prominent smooth muscle
Respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts: alveoli open off the walls
Alveoli: type I and II pneumocytes, macrophages, thin blood–air barrier, elastic septa
questions.modelAnswer: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, supported by submucosal seromucous glands and C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage joined behind by trachealis muscle. Bronchi have the same epithelium but irregular plates of cartilage and a distinct layer of smooth muscle. In bronchioles the cartilage and glands are gone, the epithelium becomes simple columnar and then cuboidal, goblet cells are replaced by club cells and smooth muscle forms a relatively thick layer. Respiratory bronchioles have alveoli opening from their walls, leading to alveolar ducts and sacs. Alveoli are lined by thin type I pneumocytes and surfactant-secreting type II pneumocytes, with macrophages in the air spaces and capillary-rich elastic septa forming a very thin barrier for gas exchange.

questions.q: In a kidney section, tubules have tall eosinophilic cells with a brush border and an indistinct lumen. Which segment is this?
options: Thin limb of the loop of Henle
questions.why: The brush border, mitochondria-rich eosinophilic cytoplasm and fuzzy lumen identify the proximal tubule. Distal tubules lack a brush border and have clear lumens, thin limbs are lined by squamous cells and collecting ducts have paler cells with distinct boundaries.

questions.q: Which zone of the adrenal cortex is the main source of cortisol?
questions.why: Cortisol comes mainly from the large lipid-laden cells of the zona fasciculata. The glomerulosa makes aldosterone, the reticularis makes mainly adrenal androgens, and the medulla secretes catecholamines.

questions.q: Describe the structure of the adrenal gland and relate each region to its secretion.
markScheme: Capsule; cortex (mesoderm) and medulla (neural crest)
Zona glomerulosa: clusters under capsule, aldosterone
Zona fasciculata: thick, columns of lipid-laden pale cells, cortisol
Zona reticularis: network of eosinophilic cords, androgens
Medulla: chromaffin cells, adrenaline/noradrenaline, preganglionic sympathetic innervation; cortical blood flow raises cortisol which favours adrenaline synthesis
questions.modelAnswer: The adrenal gland has a connective tissue capsule, an outer cortex derived from mesoderm and an inner medulla derived from neural crest. Just under the capsule, the zona glomerulosa has small cells in rounded clusters that secrete aldosterone. The zona fasciculata, the thickest layer, consists of long columns of large pale cells full of lipid droplets, which secrete cortisol. The innermost zona reticularis is a network of cords of smaller, more eosinophilic cells that produce adrenal androgens. The medulla contains chromaffin cells, modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons that are innervated by preganglionic fibres and secrete adrenaline and noradrenaline. Blood drains from the cortex into the medulla, exposing chromaffin cells to high cortisol concentrations, which promote the enzyme that converts noradrenaline into adrenaline.

questions.q: A section of gut shows villi, numerous goblet cells and large aggregates of lymphoid follicles extending into the submucosa. Which region is it?
questions.why: Villi place it in the small intestine, and Peyer's patches identify the ileum. The duodenum is distinguished by Brunner's glands, the colon has no villi and the stomach has gastric pits and glands, not villi.

questions.q: Autoimmune destruction of which cell type leads to vitamin B12 deficiency?
questions.why: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which is required for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Chief cells make pepsinogen, Brunner's glands make alkaline mucus and Paneth cells make antimicrobial proteins.

questions.q: Explain how the structure of the small intestine is adapted for absorption.
markScheme: Surface area amplified by plicae circulares, villi and microvilli (brush border)
Enterocytes: columnar cells with brush border enzymes and transporters; tight junctions
Lamina propria of villi: capillaries (to portal blood) and lacteals (lipid as chylomicrons)
Crypt stem cells renew epithelium every few days; Paneth cells protect stem cell niche
Motility from muscularis externa mixes contents; goblet cells provide protective mucus
questions.modelAnswer: The small intestine maximises absorptive surface at three levels: plicae circulares (permanent folds of mucosa and submucosa), villi (finger-like projections of the mucosa) and microvilli forming the brush border on each enterocyte. Enterocytes are tall columnar cells whose brush border carries digestive enzymes and transporters, joined by tight junctions that control paracellular movement. Each villus has a core of lamina propria containing a capillary network, which drains absorbed sugars and amino acids into the portal circulation, and a central lacteal that carries absorbed fat as chylomicrons. Stem cells in the crypts renew the epithelium every few days, while Paneth cells secrete antimicrobial proteins, and goblet cells provide protective mucus. Contractions of the muscularis externa mix the contents and bring them into contact with the surface.

questions.q: Which feature most reliably distinguishes the exocrine pancreas from the parotid gland?
options: Presence of islets and centroacinar cells, with no striated ducts
questions.why: Both glands have serous acini with zymogen granules and intercalated ducts, so those do not separate them. The pancreas has islets and centroacinar cells and lacks striated ducts, whereas the parotid has prominent striated ducts.

questions.q: In the liver acinus model, why are hepatocytes in zone 3 most susceptible to ischaemic damage?
options: They receive blood last, after oxygen has been taken up by cells upstream
They are nearest the hepatic arteriole
They are separated from the sinusoids by a thick basement membrane
questions.why: Blood enters at the portal tracts (zone 1) and flows towards the central vein, so zone 3 cells receive the least oxygenated blood. They are farthest from, not nearest, the hepatic arteriole, they have plenty of mitochondria, and hepatic sinusoids lack a proper basement membrane.

questions.q: Describe the arrangement of hepatocytes, blood vessels and bile channels in the liver, and explain how the direction of flow relates to the acinus concept.
markScheme: Hepatocyte plates 1–2 cells thick between sinusoids
Sinusoids: fenestrated, discontinuous endothelium, Kupffer cells, space of Disse with stellate cells
Blood from portal vein and hepatic artery flows through sinusoids to central vein
Bile in canaliculi between hepatocytes flows in opposite direction to portal tract bile ducts
Acinus: zone 1 periportal (best oxygenated) to zone 3 centrilobular (least oxygenated; vulnerable to hypoxia and some toxins)
questions.modelAnswer: Hepatocytes are arranged in plates one to two cells thick that radiate between portal tracts and central veins. Between the plates are sinusoids lined by fenestrated, discontinuous endothelium without a proper basement membrane, with Kupffer cells on their walls. The space of Disse separates the endothelium from the hepatocytes and contains stellate cells. Blood from branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery in the portal tracts mixes in the sinusoids and flows towards the central vein. Bile is secreted into canaliculi formed between adjacent hepatocytes and flows in the opposite direction, towards bile ducts in the portal tracts. The acinus concept describes the unit supplied by one portal tract: hepatocytes in zone 1 near the portal tract receive the best-oxygenated blood, whereas zone 3 near the central vein receives the least oxygen and has the most drug-metabolising enzymes, making it most vulnerable to ischaemia and certain toxins.

questions.q: Which pituitary cell type would you classify as a basophil on routine staining?
questions.why: Corticotrophs (ACTH), thyrotrophs and gonadotrophs are basophils. Somatotrophs and lactotrophs are acidophils, and pituicytes are glial cells of the posterior pituitary.

questions.q: Where is antidiuretic hormone synthesised?
options: In neuronal cell bodies in the hypothalamus
In acidophils of the anterior pituitary
In pituicytes of the posterior pituitary
In zona glomerulosa cells of the adrenal
questions.why: ADH is made by neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and transported down their axons to be stored and released in the posterior pituitary. Pituicytes are supporting glial cells, anterior pituitary acidophils make growth hormone and prolactin, and the zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone.

questions.q: Describe the histology of the thyroid gland and explain how it changes when the gland is stimulated by TSH.
markScheme: Follicles of simple cuboidal epithelium surrounding colloid (thyroglobulin)
Rich fenestrated capillary network between follicles
Parafollicular C cells secrete calcitonin
Stimulation: follicular cells become taller, colloid reduced and scalloped (endocytosis)
Mechanism: thyroglobulin iodinated in colloid, reabsorbed and processed in lysosomes to release T4/T3
questions.modelAnswer: The thyroid is made of spherical follicles lined by simple cuboidal follicular cells and filled with eosinophilic colloid, which is stored thyroglobulin. A dense network of fenestrated capillaries surrounds the follicles, and paler parafollicular C cells, which secrete calcitonin, lie between them. Follicular cells synthesise thyroglobulin, and iodide is oxidised and attached to its tyrosine residues within the colloid. Under TSH stimulation the cells take colloid back up by endocytosis and digest it in lysosomes to release T4 and T3 into the blood. A stimulated gland therefore shows taller, columnar follicular cells and smaller amounts of colloid with scalloped edges where it is being resorbed, while an inactive gland has flattened cells and large follicles full of colloid.

questions.q: Discuss how the structure of epithelia at different sites reflects their function, using the respiratory tract, the kidney and the gut as examples.
markScheme: General properties: polarity, junctions, basement membrane, avascularity
Respiratory: pseudostratified ciliated with goblet cells for mucociliary clearance; change to cuboidal/club cells in bronchioles; thin type I pneumocytes for diffusion; type II for surfactant
Kidney: podocytes and filtration slits; PCT brush border and mitochondria for bulk reabsorption; DCT/collecting duct regulated transport; urothelium for stretch and impermeability
Gut: stratified squamous in oesophagus and anal canal for abrasion; columnar mucus-secreting stomach; absorptive enterocytes with microvilli; colonic goblet cells; crypt stem cells for renewal
Clinical examples of failure or metaplasia (e.g. smokers' squamous metaplasia, Barrett's oesophagus, coeliac villous atrophy)
Clear linking of structure to function throughout
questions.modelAnswer:
Epithelia share core features: they are sheets of polarised cells resting on a basement membrane, joined by tight junctions, adherens junctions and desmosomes, and nourished by diffusion from underlying connective tissue. Within this plan, the number of layers, cell shape and surface specialisations vary to suit local function.

In the respiratory tract the conducting airways must clean the air. The trachea and bronchi are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells; mucus traps particles and coordinated ciliary beating moves it towards the pharynx. In bronchioles the epithelium becomes simple cuboidal, goblet cells give way to club cells, which secrete protective proteins and replace damaged cells, and smooth muscle regulates airway calibre. In the alveoli the requirement is diffusion, so type I pneumocytes are extremely thin, forming a blood–air barrier less than a micrometre thick, while type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant to reduce surface tension. When smoking damages the airways, ciliated epithelium can undergo squamous metaplasia, which is more resistant but loses mucociliary clearance.

The kidney shows how epithelia specialise for filtration and transport. Podocytes wrap glomerular capillaries with interdigitating foot processes; their slit diaphragms, with the basement membrane and fenestrated endothelium, filter plasma by size and charge. Proximal tubule cells reabsorb most of the filtrate, and accordingly have a dense brush border to increase surface area, many mitochondria to power sodium pumping, and basal infoldings. Distal tubule and collecting duct cells have fewer microvilli but are hormonally regulated: principal cells insert aquaporin-2 in response to antidiuretic hormone. Downstream, urothelium lines the ureter and bladder; its surface cells flatten as the bladder fills and form a barrier to the toxic contents of urine.

In the gut, the oesophagus and anal canal face abrasion and are lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium. The stomach surface is protected from its own acid by simple columnar cells secreting thick alkaline mucus, while its glands contain specialised secretory cells. The small intestine is lined by tall enterocytes whose microvilli, with villi and circular folds, greatly enlarge the absorptive surface; goblet cells lubricate and Paneth cells defend the crypts. The colon lacks villi but has many goblet cells to lubricate increasingly solid contents. Rapid renewal from crypt stem cells replaces cells lost every few days. Function fails when structure changes: villous atrophy in coeliac disease reduces absorption, and Barrett's oesophagus replaces squamous epithelium with columnar epithelium in response to acid.

Across these systems, therefore, epithelial structure closely matches function: thin where diffusion is needed, folded and microvillous where absorption is needed, stratified where abrasion is a risk, and ciliated where material must be moved.

questions.q: Compare the histological organisation of an exocrine gland and an endocrine gland, using the pancreas, salivary glands, thyroid and adrenal gland as examples.
markScheme: Exocrine: secretory units (acini/tubules) plus duct system; serous vs mucous cells; myoepithelial cells
Salivary: parotid serous, sublingual mainly mucous, submandibular mixed; intercalated, striated and excretory ducts; striated ducts modify saliva
Pancreas: serous acini with zymogen granules, centroacinar cells, no striated ducts; islets as endocrine component
Endocrine: no ducts, cords/clusters/follicles with fenestrated capillaries
Thyroid stores hormone extracellularly in colloid; adrenal cortex makes steroids on demand (lipid droplets, smooth ER, mitochondria) and medulla stores catecholamines in granules
Mixed gland example and clear comparison of storage and secretion strategies
questions.modelAnswer:
Exocrine glands release secretions onto an epithelial surface through ducts, whereas endocrine glands release hormones into the blood and have no ducts. This difference shapes their histology.

Exocrine glands consist of secretory end-pieces drained by branching ducts. In salivary glands the end-pieces are either serous, with round, basally placed nuclei and granular cytoplasm that is basophilic at the base, or mucous, with pale foamy cytoplasm and flattened basal nuclei. The parotid is almost purely serous, the submandibular is mixed with a serous majority and the sublingual is mainly mucous. Myoepithelial cells around the end-pieces contract to expel secretion. Secretions pass into intercalated ducts lined by low cuboidal cells, then striated ducts, whose columnar cells have basal infoldings packed with mitochondria and reabsorb sodium chloride, making saliva hypotonic, and finally into larger excretory ducts.

The exocrine pancreas follows a similar plan but with important differences. Its acini are serous, with intensely basophilic basal cytoplasm full of rough ER and apical eosinophilic zymogen granules containing enzymes or proenzymes. Centroacinar cells, the start of the duct system, sit inside the acini and, with duct cells, secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid. There are no striated ducts. Scattered among the acini are pale islets of Langerhans, so the pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine gland.

Endocrine glands are organised for rapid exchange with the blood. Their cells are in cords, clusters or follicles closely related to fenestrated capillaries. The islets of Langerhans are clusters of beta, alpha, delta and PP cells with a dense capillary network. The thyroid is unusual in storing its hormone outside cells: follicular cells surround colloid made of thyroglobulin, which is iodinated in the lumen and then taken back into the cell by endocytosis and digested to release thyroxine and triiodothyronine. Its appearance therefore changes with activity, with taller cells and less colloid when stimulated.

The adrenal gland shows two other strategies. Cortical cells make steroid hormones, which are lipid-soluble and are not stored in granules but synthesised on demand from cholesterol. These cells have abundant smooth ER, mitochondria with tubular cristae and lipid droplets, which give the zona fasciculata its foamy look. The zones are arranged as clusters (glomerulosa), straight cords (fasciculata) and a network (reticularis), all between sinusoidal capillaries. The medulla's chromaffin cells, derived from neural crest, store catecholamines in membrane-bound granules and release them by exocytosis in response to preganglionic sympathetic stimulation.

In summary, exocrine glands are defined by duct systems that can modify their secretion, while endocrine glands are defined by close contact with capillaries. The way endocrine cells store their products, whether in extracellular colloid, intracellular granules or not at all, is visible in their histology and links directly to the chemistry of the hormone.
